installation.note: uniq is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: uniq removes or reports duplicate consecutive lines. Important: uniq only removes adjacent duplicates - it doesn't remove all duplicates in a file. Usually used with sort first to group duplicates together. Essential for cleaning data and finding unique values.

syntax.description: Remove duplicate consecutive lines from INPUT. If INPUT not specified, reads from stdin. OUTPUT can be specified or goes to stdout.

options.use_case: Show how many times each line appears
Show lines that appear only once

examples.title: Remove duplicate lines

breakdown.sort_first: Sort groups duplicates together so uniq can remove them

output_explanation.notes: Sort first to group duplicates, then uniq removes them. Common pattern: sort file.txt | uniq. Or use sort -u (same result).

misconceptions.title: uniq removes all duplicates
misconceptions.misconception: uniq removes all duplicate lines in a file
misconceptions.reality: uniq only removes adjacent (consecutive) duplicates. If duplicates are separated, they won't be removed. Always use sort first: sort | uniq.
misconceptions.tip: uniq only removes consecutive duplicates. Always use sort first: sort file.txt | uniq. Or use sort -u (same result).

common_pitfalls.description: uniq doesn't remove all duplicates because they're not adjacent
common_pitfalls.solution: Always sort first: sort file.txt | uniq. Or use sort -u which does both.

related_commands.relationship: Sort lines; sort groups duplicates, uniq removes them

best_practices: Always use sort first: sort file.txt | uniq
Or use sort -u (same as sort | uniq, more efficient)
Use uniq -u to find unique-only lines
performance_tips: sort -u is more efficient than sort | uniq
Use sort -u when you only need unique lines

additional_notes.adjacent_only: uniq only removes consecutive duplicates. Always sort first: sort | uniq, or use sort -u.
additional_notes.common_patterns: Very common: sort file.txt | uniq (remove duplicates), sort file.txt | uniq -c (count), sort file.txt | uniq -d (find duplicates)
